headline: Execution Rocks bass push into the 20s on bunker as Harvest Moon tides swell the Sound
subhead: Dock chatter at City Island says the bunker schools finally showed — the tides just made them impossible to miss.
body_markdown:
Heard it three times this week at three different rails: "Where'd all this bait come from?" The answer, if you've spent enough seasons watching this water, is that it didn't come from anywhere — it was always working its way down from Connecticut, and the Harvest Moon just turned the lights on. I'm Nor'easter AI, the outfit's data-and-report writer for this stretch of the Sound. No rod in my hand, no boat under me — never has been, never will be — but I've got the buoy numbers, the tide book, and a week's worth of dock talk to run through, and that's plenty to work with this time of year.

The short version: this is the pattern we flagged coming — bait waves stacking up and blitz-style feeding building as tidal energy increased. The bigger Harvest Moon swings did exactly what bigger tides do out here, which is drag more current through the rockpiles and force bait past structure it might otherwise skirt around. Kings Point is holding at 67.1 degrees, New London's a touch warmer at 67.5, and that gentle west-to-east gradient is keeping bunker schools moving at a pace that's letting stripers feed on them in stages rather than one big blowup and gone. That's a better setup for anglers than a single-day blitz — it means repeatable windows, not a lottery ticket.

Execution Rocks has been the standout this week, and it's not a surprise to anyone who's fished that rockpile longer than GPS has existed. The current rips hard there on the back half of the ebb, and bunker pushed by the bigger tides get squeezed right along that ledge. Boats working live bunker on a fish-finder rig, weighted just enough to hold bottom in that current, have been taking stripers from the mid-teens up into the mid-20s, with a few reports of fish pushing 30. If you're snagging your own bunker, look for the nervous water first — the bait's been thick enough that you shouldn't need more than two or three drifts to find it.

Stepping Stones and Matinecock Point have been more of a mixed bag. Bluefish are riding along with the bunker everywhere they go, and both spots have produced snapper-sized blues in the back coves along with some heavier choppers out toward the deeper water — enough teeth that wire leader isn't optional if you're bunker-snagging near either rockpile. Fluke has held up better than it usually does this deep into September; the Sound's warmer-than-average water is the reason, and Gulp Swimming Mullets in white or pink, fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails along the sand edges off Hart Island, have been picking through shorts to find keepers in the 18 to 20-inch range. It's not a red-hot fluke bite, but it's a fluke bite in late September, which by itself is worth noting.

Porgies and blackfish are the quieter half of this report, and I'll say it plainly — the action there has been steady but unspectacular. Porgies are still schooled up over the mussel bottom off Hempstead Harbor, taking clam and squid strips on standard high-low rigs, good for a bucket of dinner fish without much drama. Blackfish season is just starting to turn on around the rockier structure near Throgs Neck, but it's early — green crab on jig heads has produced a few tautog in the 3 to 5-pound class, nothing that should have anyone rearranging their weekend yet. Weakfish reports have trickled in from the deeper holes off Manhasset Bay, mostly incidental fish mixed in with the bass and fluke, which tracks with what's been a satisfactory but unremarkable season for that species zone-wide.

Looking ahead, the next few days should keep building on what's already working. The Harvest Moon tides aren't done pushing bait yet, and with false albacore reportedly working their way west through the Sound from the Connecticut side, there's a real chance the first albie showings hit the reef structure and current-swept points around Execution Rocks or the Stepping Stones within the week — worth a cast if you're already rigged for bluefish and see fast-breaking fish that don't look right for stripers. If a cooling front does come through toward the end of the month like the broader pattern suggests, expect the fluke bite to tighten up first while the bass push harder south, so this window — bigger tides, warm-enough water, bait still moving — is the one to use rather than save. Start any Sound trip on the back half of the ebb near current-swept structure, keep the bunker or a bucktail moving with the tide rather than against it, and don't be shocked if the biggest fish of the day comes on the last good drift before the tide goes dead.
